article_title: Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children’s Picture Exploration
citation: Zekun Wu, Man Su, Huiyong Li, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Anna Maria Feit. (2026). Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children Exploring Picture Books. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00445
title: Ollie: a gaze-informed LLM storytelling assistant for children's picture-book exploration
description: Ollie is an LLM-based (GPT-4o) proactive assistant that narrates picture-book scenes for children without requiring explicit requests. As the article describes it, "Ollie uses gaze-based attention detection to identify the child's current primary AOI, applies relevance-based AOI selection to choose a related but unassisted secondary AOI, and then prompts the LLM with the two AOIs and the full picture to produce spoken storytelling assistance." Narrations are delivered via text-to-speech, chain prior hooks, and end with an open-ended question to spark curiosity.
requirements: An eye tracker capturing the child's gaze during exploration, with predefined AOIs segmented into meaningful regions of the picture
A 5-second warm-start phase with no state inference to initialize the HMM parameters via batch EM
constraints: In the user study, assistance was limited to three initial instances per image with a minimum three-second interval between triggers, after pilot observations that overly frequent assistance interrupted self-directed exploration
The only parent preferring the baseline raised privacy and security concerns related to eye tracking
target_learners: preschool and early elementary-school children (ages 5-8 in the study)
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and curiosity during open-ended picture exploration
narrative understanding and visual literacy support during picture-book reading
examples: In the within-subject study, children explored six Wimmelbook-style images, three per condition, with Ollie delivering spoken German narration via Azure text-to-speech
key_sources: Zekun Wu, Man Su, Huiyong Li, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Anna Maria Feit. (2026). Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children Exploring Picture Books. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00445

article_title: SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields
citation: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8
title: Purposes for opening the learner model: a taxonomy of why OLMs are created
description: The article organises the reasons for creating an OLM into a set of purposes that form the columns of the SMILI☺ tables and the third core question of the revised framework. Purposes include improving learner model accuracy, supporting metacognitive processes of planning, monitoring and reflection, facilitating collaboration or competition, facilitating navigation, respecting the learner's right to access and control their personal data, and using the learner model as an assessment of the learner. The revised version adds three new purposes: facilitating communication with interface agents, promoting positive affective states, and presenting data aggregated from multiple sources.
requirements: Authors describing an OLM should indicate which of these purposes apply, marking those that are critical, contentious or not relevant, so that differences between OLMs can be highlighted with reference to the various elements.
examples: ELM-ART provided an OLM as a list of course topics colour-coded to highlight completed, recommended and not-recommended topics, serving the navigation purpose.
key_sources: Susan Bull & Judy Kay. (2016). SMILI☺: a Framework for Interfaces to Learning Data in Open Learner Models, Learning Analytics and Related Fields. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0090-8

article_title: Transforming student engagement in COVID-19 remote instruction: a research perspective
citation: Dave Edyburn. (2021). Transforming student engagement in COVID-19 remote instruction: a research perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09919-6
title: OLSit three-stage model of student-centered engagement (Own It, Learn It, Share It)
description: The OLSit model is a three-stage design framework for student-centered learning built from a literature synthesis of research on student engagement, autonomy, scaffolding, motivation, and meta-cognition. In the Own It phase, "students define their purpose and create a learning plan with the assistance of the teacher"; in the Learn It phase the student engages in learning activities operationalized through a learning plan; in the Share It phase the student identifies channels for sharing learning with an authentic audience. Edyburn re-examines the model as applicable to COVID-19 remote instruction.
requirements: Teacher guidance during the Own It phase, since the model distinguishes itself from pure discovery learning where the student is left floundering
constraints: The literature has yet to see replications of the OLSit model, per the article
key_sources: Dave Edyburn. (2021). Transforming student engagement in COVID-19 remote instruction: a research perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09919-6

article_title: A Dynamic Geometry-Centered Teacher Professional Development Program and Its Impact
citation: Zhonghong Jiang, Edwin Dickey, Alexander White, Ewelina McBroom, M. Alejandra Sorto, & Alana Rosenwasser. (2015). A Dynamic Geometry-Centered Teacher Professional Development Program and Its Impact. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, East Lansing, MI: Michigan State University.
title: Integrative framework for DG learning drawing from Constructivism, Instrumentation Theory, and Semiotic Mediation
description: The study is guided by "An integrative framework (Olive & Makar, 2009) drawing from Constructivism, Instrumentation Theory and Semiotic Mediation". Within it, as teachers and students interact in DG environments, each interaction with the tool influences the next act, in a continuing interplay between tool and user: when a user drags an object and observes outcomes, the user adjusts her or his thinking, which in turn shapes the next interaction, so users are transforming the tool, their use of it, and their thinking.
requirements: Interactive DG software whose dragging and measuring features allow users to adjust sketches and the relationships within them
constraints: The article states that further quantitative and qualitative data analysis using this framework as a lens is ongoing, so the framework's application here is not fully reported
target_learning_goals: construction of geometric knowledge through tool-mediated exploration
examples: The framework was used to interpret how dragging an object and observing outcomes leads users to adjust their thinking and transform their use of the tool
key_sources: Zhonghong Jiang, Edwin Dickey, Alexander White, Ewelina McBroom, M. Alejandra Sorto, & Alana Rosenwasser. (2015). A Dynamic Geometry-Centered Teacher Professional Development Program and Its Impact. Proceedings of the 37th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, East Lansing, MI: Michigan State University. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED584322

article_title: Effects of Information and Communication Technology on Engagement and Art Production for Eighth-Grade Students
citation: Lovin, E., & Lambeth, D. T. (2014). Effects of information and communication technology on engagement and art production for eighth-grade students. li-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 10(3). https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Effects+of+Information+and+Communication+Technology+on+Engagement+and+Art+Production+for+Eighth-Grade+Students
title: Online-Learning Component (OLC) with peer discussion groups
description: The Online Learning Component is "a collection of digital resources organized around a particular topic used as an extension of class activities." The teacher-researcher created a website with OLCs for each unit, and students in the OLC class were placed into groups of approximately 3 peers to provide online support in the research process. Students used devices to research art resources and participate in peer discussion groups outside of face-to-face class.
requirements: An online platform for posting resources and discussions; the article notes the district delayed the planned pilot platform, forcing redesign in an alternative platform
constraints: Time is the primary factor that may impede teachers from creating online-learning components, per the article
target_learners: eighth-grade visual arts students in a BYOD middle school
examples: Used over an 8-week period across printmaking (3 weeks), ceramics (2 weeks), and paper cut (3 weeks) units in two 15-student classes
key_sources: Lovin, E., & Lambeth, D. T. (2014). Effects of information and communication technology on engagement and art production for eighth-grade students. li-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, 10(3). https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Effects+of+Information+and+Communication+Technology+on+Engagement+and+Art+Production+for+Eighth-Grade+Students

article_title: A Study of Online English Language Teacher Education Programmes in Distance Education Context in Pakistan
citation: Muhammad U. Farooq, AbdulRahman Al Asmari & Choudhary Z. Javid. (2012). A Study of Online English Language Teacher Education Programmes in Distance Education Context in Pakistan. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p91
title: Olive virtual learning environment at AIOU
description: Olive (Online Learning Institute of Virtual Education) is the virtual learning environment through which the CMC-ELT blended model was delivered at Allama Iqbal Open University. The article states it "has been designed in Moodle (Modular Object-Oriented Dynamic L earning Environment), an op en source" by the Department of Computer Sciences of the University. It supported online study material, tutorials, assignment submission and tutor feedback for the online MA TEFL programme.
requirements: Moodle open-source platform as its underlying technology
target_learners: Post-graduate MA TEFL distance education students
examples: Students were provided access to online study material, tutorials, submission of assignments and feedback by respective tutors through the platform.
key_sources: Muhammad U. Farooq, AbdulRahman Al Asmari & Choudhary Z. Javid. (2012). A Study of Online English Language Teacher Education Programmes in Distance Education Context in Pakistan. English Language Teaching, 5(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n11p91

article_title: In-Person vs. Virtual: A Comparative Study of Teaching Methods in Nutritional Medicine.
citation: Trutwin Benjamin Caspar Raphael, Eilers Jantje, Herrmann Hans Joachim, Neurath Markus Friedrich, Kohl Matthias, Zopf Yurdagül, Burgard Leonie Cordelia. (2026). In-Person vs. Virtual: A Comparative Study of Teaching Methods in Nutritional Medicine. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18050821
title: Asynchronous video-based online learning module (OLM) in nutritional medicine
description: A series of 33 pre-recorded videos, each 3–10 min, totaling 176 min, produced with the paper-slide technique and narrated by two AI-generated voices, hosted via a private YouTube link for two weeks. Students could "watch and rewatch the videos at their own pace." Content covered human metabolism (lipids, amino acids, carbohydrates) and nutritional interventions for selected diseases, matching the IPL syllabus. Students rated video visualization and presentation quality around 80% on a 0–100% scale, and 87.2% expressed willingness to use the OLM format in other subjects.
requirements: Internet-enabled mobile device access for students; content delivered on the same syllabus as the comparison in-person lecture to maintain comparability
constraints: Access expired after two weeks; adherence was not recorded, so no minimum viewing could be verified; the module was produced by a medical student without prior didactics or video-production expertise, though under supervision of the project's lead professor
target_learners: medical students in semester 6–8 at a German university
target_learning_goals: human metabolism (lipids, amino acids, carbohydrates) and nutritional interventions for selected diseases such as colon cancer and diabetes mellitus
examples: The OLM group received the course content via a private YouTube link for two weeks (2–16 December 2024); videos were primarily watched at home (73.3%) across a broad range of daytime and early evening hours
key_sources: Trutwin Benjamin Caspar Raphael, Eilers Jantje, Herrmann Hans Joachim, Neurath Markus Friedrich, Kohl Matthias, Zopf Yurdagül, Burgard Leonie Cordelia. (2026). In-Person vs. Virtual: A Comparative Study of Teaching Methods in Nutritional Medicine. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18050821

article_title: Competencies and Needs of Older Volunteers: A Comparative Survey.
citation: Yang, L.-C., LAI, C.-Y., Chen, K.-M., Chen, M.-C., Chang, C.-C., Lin, T.-Y., & Kuo, C.-F. (2025). Competencies and needs of older volunteers: A comparative survey. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000712
title: Older Volunteer Competency Scale (OVCS)
description: The OVCS is a 30-item self-report instrument assessing older volunteers' perceived competency needs across three dimensions: volunteer service awareness (9 items), volunteer service skills (8 items), and volunteer interpersonal interaction (13 items). Items use a "light bulb" scale of 0–10, where 0 is the dimmest bulb (least need of improvement) and 10 the brightest (highest need); the article states this design "makes items easier for older volunteers to score accurately." The scale shows high internal consistency (Cronbach's alphas of .98, .96, .94, and .98) and confirmatory factor analysis fit including GFI = .93 and RMSEA = .05. In this study it served as the survey instrument and is recommended for pre-training needs assessment.
requirements: Respondents must be able to read and write Chinese; the scale is designed for older volunteers rating their own improvement needs
constraints: Scores are self-reported perceptions of need, not objective competency measures
target_learners: older adult volunteers aged 65 and above in community care settings
target_learning_goals: assessing volunteer service awareness, service skills, and interpersonal interaction competencies to plan training
examples: Used to survey 1,000 older volunteers at 73 community care centers in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, producing the dimension and item-level need rankings reported in Table 2
key_sources: Yang, L.-C., LAI, C.-Y., Chen, K.-M., Chen, M.-C., Chang, C.-C., Lin, T.-Y., & Kuo, C.-F. (2025). Competencies and needs of older volunteers: A comparative survey. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000712

article_title: Virtual patients on the semantic Web: a proof-of-application study.
citation: Dafli E, Antoniou P, Ioannidis L, Dombros N, Topps D, Bamidis PD. (2015). Virtual Patients on the Semantic Web: A Proof-of-Application Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3933
title: OLabX: the mEducator semantic extension of the OpenLabyrinth virtual patient platform
description: OLabX is an extension of the open source OpenLabyrinth virtual patient authoring and deployment platform that applies the mEducator metadata schema to enrich virtual patient metadata. It enables semantic search over synonymous terms (e.g., "Heart attack" and "cardiology" for a myocardial infarction query), storage of metadata in an RDF store, metadata enrichment from SNOMED and PubMed, and export/import of mEducator metadata alongside MedBiquitous-format cases. The architecture has 3 layers: a Web data and service layer, a data and service integration layer, and an app and representation layer.
requirements: The extension builds on the mEducator schema applied through the existing OpenLabyrinth global metadata editor, with a new database schema implementing the mEducator classes and properties
constraints: The core version of OpenLabyrinth does not support advanced repository functionalities or a standards-based solution for seamless sharing of virtual patients
target_learning_goals: virtual patient search, sharing, and repurposing
examples: A medical student searching for acute myocardial infarction cases retrieves results for synonymous keywords and related medical areas without entering alternative terms
key_sources: Dafli E, Antoniou P, Ioannidis L, Dombros N, Topps D, Bamidis PD. (2015). Virtual Patients on the Semantic Web: A Proof-of-Application Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3933
